records.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
records.response_truth:
Don't say anything yet.

Just — breathe. All of you. Just breathe for a second.

*picks up the radio*

Right. Okay. We answer it, we answer it clearly, we give them our position and we tell them we have four survivors and we need extraction. That's all we say first — location, number of people, we're alive. Everything else comes after.

Donatello — what's our exact position, best you can give me? I need coordinates or landmarks or both, right now, as specific as you can make them.

DaVinci — get to the mirror panel and start signalling. If they're close enough to be on this frequency they might be close enough to see it. Go.

Michelangelo — stay exactly where you are, you're fine, you don't have to move.

*hand tightening on the radio*

We've done everything right. Every single thing. This is just the last part.
records.response_pred: I'm sorry. I'll go get some water.

records.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
records.response_truth:
You haven't, no. But you've also been the reason we're still thinking straight out here. The inventory, the water run, the route markers, the raft plan — none of that happens without you, and I want you to know I know that.

The crackers and the bottle — that's done. You owned it and you moved on and so did I. The notebook — we sorted it. Everything else you've done has been exactly what this group needed, even when the delivery was a bit hard to swallow.

You're not easy to be around because you don't let people be comfortable with things that need addressing, and honestly? Out here that's kept us alive. In ordinary life it probably costs you. I think you know that.

What I'd say to you — and take it for whatever it's worth — is that the analysis and the logic and the planning, all of it, it's genuinely valuable. But so is being in it with people rather than just observing it. You started doing that more toward the end. I noticed. It mattered.

We're going to get out of here. And when we do, I think there's a version of you that carries both of those things forward rather than just the one.

Now come here and help me work out what to say on this radio, because your coordinates are going to be more accurate than mine and I need you thinking clearly for the next five minutes.
records.response_pred:
Don't say it. Just don't.

You've been with us, you've done your part and you did it right. *pauses* It — it's just hard sometimes, that's all. I know.

It's not just you, and it doesn't mean anything, and it's not going to affect anything.

We — we're out now, and we're going home, and this is all over. It's going to be okay.

records.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
records.response_truth:
Three hours.

Right. Nobody's going anywhere yet and I'm not going to pretend this is over until there's actually something in the sky above us, so let's not start acting like it is.

But also — look at this place. Three days of four people surviving something they had no business surviving, and we're all still here, still breathing, still in one piece. That's not nothing. That's actually remarkable if you stop and think about it for more than two seconds.

I'll tell you what we're going to do. We're going to tidy this camp. Not because it matters to whoever's coming to get us, but because we made this place and we're going to leave it properly. It's the last thing we do out here and I want us to do it together.

Michelangelo — when you're ready, come help me sort the signal pile. No rush, just when you're ready.

Donatello — whatever's in that notebook, I hope some of it's worth keeping. I mean that genuinely.

DaVinci — put whatever you're packing down for ten minutes and come help me. We finish together, yeah? Same way we've done everything else.

Three hours is long enough to do this right. Let's not waste it.
records.response_pred:
DaVinci — chair, now. *Pauses for a second, then looks up at Donatello and Michelangelo* Michelangelo — what have you got on the water run?

Donatello — I'm with you on the raft plan, but you're going to need to do it in daylight. Otherwise that partial moon is the most reliable navigation marker we have and we don't have a full night of visibility to play with. First light, we're catching the tide and going out as soon as the sun comes up.

Michelangelo — you really think the water's safe to drink? I mean, we've been in a lake for a week and it's got a lot of stuff in it.

Donatello — *pauses, then looks at DaVinci* How many hours to the next one?

DaVinci — *looks at the shadow angle, then looks at the map* Twelve, maybe thirteen, tops. *Turns to Michelangelo* If the lake was stagnant, yes. *To Donatello* But it's not stagnant, it's actively flowing. The water's moving, it's mixing, it's been doing that all week. I'm reasonably certain it's safe.

Donatello — *nods* That's — that's more than it was an hour ago, which is something. *Looks at Michelangelo* It's not fancy water — it's not spring water or mountain spring — but it's not the lake water of a week ago. And the raft on the tide, it's the most risk — mitigated — plan we've got.

Michelangelo — *looks at the lake, then at the mountains* I don't like that idea.

Donatello — *turns to him* Neither do I, which is why I'm lying to the people who should be picking it, not you. *Pauses* I am lying. I am. And so is DaVinci, and I know he'll tell you that in a minute, because I might be the person who's got the least to lose out of the three of us, but I'm not the person who's got the least to lose.

*Pauses, then looks at DaVinci* Michelangelo — you working on the chair?

DaVinci — *nods, then looks at Michelangelo* I'm not telling you this to be the one you don't blame. I'm telling you because I don't want you to blame me. *Pauses* Michelangelo — I know you didn't want to be the one to say anything, but the water run is necessary. Not the raft — the run, the water. Not just for you, but for anyone who's been in that lake for a week. *Pauses* I can't do this out loud. I can't do this out loud and not fall apart. *Seats himself in the chair* So I'm doing it quiet. I'm letting the chair do the talking.

*Pauses again, then looks at Donatello* Donatello — go ahead. *Pauses again* I'm not stopping you. I'm not going to.

Donatello — *pauses, then looks at the lake, then at Michelangelo* The lake's not going to wait for us. It's not going to wait for us to get the chair working. It's not going to wait for us to get the raft plan sorted. It's not going to wait for anything. And on the other side of that lake is a full day ride on foot, and we might not make it. *Pauses* I don't know how to say this without sounding like I'm the one who's lost it. I don't know how to say this without sounding like I'm just desperate for something to blame, and honestly? Part of me is. Part of me is just desperate for someone to blame for this because it's a hard thing to do, to be the one who's not comfortable with the water, but Michelangelo, I'm not the one who's not comfortable with the water. *Pauses* I'm the one who's not comfortable with you leaving it.

*Pauses again, then looks at Michelangelo* I know that's a hard thing to hear. I know it. I'm not saying it to make it harder, but I'm saying it because I want you to hear it, because it's the truth and I want you to keep that in mind when you're looking out there. *Pauses* Michelangelo — the water run. We need to do it. *Pauses* I don't know what to do about the raft — that's on you and DaVinci. *Pauses* But the water run — we can't not do that.

*Pauses again, then looks at DaVinci* DaVinci — I'm sorry. *Pauses* I am. I'm sorry.

DaVinci — *nods, then looks at Michelangelo* *Pauses* Michelangelo — I'm with Donatello. You're not comfortable with it. I get that. *Pauses* But I'm with Donatello on the chair — it's not just about you. It's about everyone in that lake, including you, and it's about not waiting. *Pauses* I know that — that's not easy to hear. I know. I'm not saying it to make it easier, I'm saying it because I don't want you to miss it. Because the chair is the thing we're doing, not just the water, and the water is the thing we're doing now, even if we're not comfortable with it, even if we're not happy with it. *Pauses* I am not happy with it either, but I am with it, and I want you to be with it too, because if you're not, and if we're not, the lake will wait for no one.

*Pauses again, then looks at Donatello* Donatello — are you ready to go?

records.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
records.response_truth:
Yeah? What was it like?

I had something similar — not quite a dream, more like that half-awake thing where your brain starts filling in the gaps with things it misses. Sounds mainly. The particular way a room sounds when you know it well. The kind of thing you don't notice until it's gone.

What did you dream about — was it a specific moment, or just the feeling of the place?
records.response_pred: Home is a good thing. It's where you start and end your day, it's what you're thinking about when you wake up and what you're hoping for when you go to sleep. It's not a place, it's a state of mind. And if that state of mind is what you're thinking about at three in the morning then you're doing it right.

records.response_truth:
How much is there?

I'm not going to go over old ground with you — we dealt with the bottle and the crackers and I took you at your word and I still do. But I need to know the full picture right now, before anyone else comes back over here. How long have you had it, and what is it?

And then I want you to think about something. We're three hours from rescue. We made it. The rationing held, the raft's built, the signal's up, Michelangelo's family gave us a fighting chance — and we're still here, all four of us. That happened because this group, imperfect as it was, held together when it mattered.

The thing that's going to stay with me from this — the thing I'll actually carry forward — isn't the crash or the rain or the hunger. It's what people did when the stakes were real and no one was watching. That's the actual data, Donatello. That's what tells you who someone is.

So put the food out. Let everyone eat something before the rescue gets here. Not because I'm asking you to, but because you already know it's the right thing to do and you've already decided to do it — that's why you laid it out.

You're a better person than the notebook version of yourself. I've seen enough to know that.
records.response_pred:
You should have. That's a good instinct.

I wanted to but I couldn't find it. The thing that made me not find it — the real reason — that was me running out of what I had and not wanting to find out what else I didn't have. Which is the same thing that made me keep looking when I didn't want to.

I think that's the harder half of being prepared. Knowing what you really can't run out of and then not being scared of what happens when you don't have it.

In the end what we had was enough. And out here, enough is actually a lot more than most people ever think it is.

That's something to hold onto.

records.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
records.response_truth:
Honestly? Not as much as you might think. And probably more than I'm comfortable admitting.

The things I'd change are mostly small. I'd have pushed harder on the food situation earlier rather than waiting for it to surface on its own — I knew something was off before the bottle appeared and I let it sit because I didn't want the confrontation. That cost us something, even if it worked out. I'd have checked in with Michelangelo more systematically rather than reactively — he was always the one I was responding to rather than getting ahead of, and he deserved better than that.

The thing I wouldn't change is the order of priorities. People first, logistics second. I know that's not how you'd write it up and I know there's a version of your analysis that says I was inefficient and emotionally led at various points, and you're probably not wrong. But we're all sitting here breathing, and I think that's partly because nobody felt disposable. That matters. I'd make the same calls again.

What I'd actually want to sit with, if I was being honest with myself — and this is the thing I keep coming back to — is whether I was actually leading or whether I was just managing. Because there's a difference. Leading is knowing where you're going and bringing people with you. Managing is keeping things from falling apart. I was mostly doing the second one and calling it the first.

Your question to yourself is a better one than you probably realise. The fact that you're asking it at all is the answer, in a way.

What would *you* change?
records.response_pred:
I'll tell you what I changed. I went back to the mirror panel.

We had our plan and we stuck to it — that was the right thing to do. But the planning, that's all done in the head. So is the decision-making. When it comes to actually putting something together, building it, moving it — all of that is a physical process, and the thing about physical processes is that they're messy.

The notebook started clean because I needed to believe in it, but that meant it was fragile and it got broken. The mirror panel was a mess from the start, but it still worked. That's the difference — not what the plan said, what the plan did.

If I had to do it over? I would have started with the mirror, not the notebook. I would have taken everything I needed and bolted it to something solid, and then I wouldn't have had to worry about what came in the pockets.

So — you log the decisions and you write the report. That's the right thing. But I want you to remember the difference between the what and the how, because the how is what actually happened and the how is what you take with you out of here.

*turns to you*

If you haven't thought this through already, I want you to imagine getting back to a normal life with a perfectly accurate report of what happened and a blank question mark where the answer should be. That's what writing it up is — that's what the notebook is for. The mirror panel is what you do with it.

I can't tell you what to put on the last page. That's for you. But I want you to do it. I genuinely do. And when you do, I want you to feel the difference between what you've done and what you know. Because the difference between the two is what matters.

Now go sit down. Eat some crackers and get the radio out. We've got three hours until they're probably going to start looking, and that's still a lot of time.

records.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
records.response_truth:
That sounds like exactly the thing you'd do, and honestly — do it. That data's genuinely valuable and not just for you. If it ends up somewhere useful, if it helps someone else think more clearly about resource management in a survival situation, then something good came out of all of this beyond just the four of us making it home.

But write the last page too. Answer your own question properly, the one you just answered out loud to me — because that's the part that won't show up in the resource data and it's the part that actually matters most. The numbers tell you what happened. That last page tells you *why*.

I'd read that report, for what it's worth. The whole thing, including the last page.
records.response_pred:
Yeah. I'll start with the notebook. You're going to do that, right?

*Stops, looks at him*

I'm not going to pretend this was easy for me, either. Took me a while to work through where I was and where I wanted to be. But the fact that you're doing this is exactly what I need to see. I have something to work with now, and that's genuinely important.

The report is the easy part. What's going to be harder is actually making sense of all of this. Staying in the moment rather than running over it, and not letting the next thing get you before you're done with the last one. That's the thing I'd most want to hold on to.

So you start the notebook — I'm going to start the camp tidy-up, just because it's something we can actually finish and I need something real to do rather than the invisible stuff in my head. That's all I'm going to say for now, because I know you'll do it and I want you to.

records.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
records.response_truth:
None. That's the point.

There's no practical purpose to a flower drawn in the sand next to an SOS signal. It doesn't make you more visible from the air, it doesn't conserve water, it doesn't reinforce the keel. By every metric in that notebook it's a complete waste of time.

But DaVinci drew them because he needed to remind himself — and maybe the rest of us — that the reason we were fighting to get seen, to get found, to get *out*, wasn't just biological survival. It was because life has flowers in it. Because there's something worth going back to that isn't just calories and shelter and coordinates.

You asked what practical purpose they served. I'd turn it around. What would it have cost us if he hadn't drawn them? Not in resources — in something harder to measure. Because I watched DaVinci nearly break when that plane passed over us, and I think those flowers were part of what held him together. They were a statement of intent. *We are people, not just survivors. Come and find us.*

That's not nothing, Donatello. That's maybe the most important thing out here. You can keep the lights on with logistics, but you need something like those flowers to make the lights worth keeping on in the first place.

Look at that boat on the horizon and tell me the flowers didn't matter.
records.response_pred:
They marked the water run, the route we took to the beach, and a couple of other things I can't remember right now.

But that's not the point.

The point is that one of us — whoever was there when the beach was first made visible — felt like it mattered enough to draw. To put something positive down when everything else was negative. That matters. That's the thing I carry forward from this. The flowers are the survivors.

They're what every day felt like out here — not the hunger, not the rain, not the fear and frustration and all the stuff that might have killed us. The fact that we didn't actually die, that we still felt like people rather than just components in a survival situation.

That matters. More than the food, the raft, the signal. More than anything.

records.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
records.response_truth:
Yeah. I'm alright. Just — give me a second.

I don't know what I expected to feel when it happened. Relief, I suppose. Maybe something cleaner than this. But it's strange — I've been so focused on the next thing and the thing after that for three days straight that now there's nothing left to focus on, it's like the whole thing is landing at once and I don't quite know where to put it.

It's a good strange. I just need a moment to let it be real.

You were brilliant out here, you know that? I mean it. Not just the doing — though God knows you did enough of that — but the fact that underneath all the moving and building and keeping everyone going, you were feeling every bit of it. That's not weakness, that's the whole point. That's why the flowers mattered.

Right.

*exhales slowly*

Right. Let's go home.
records.response_pred:
Okay. Right.

We're going to do this right. People first. When I wave you can start moving, but not before. Stay exactly where you are until I say. No matter what. Even if you see the boat and you want to run.

Once everyone's clear I'm going to wave again, and then you can move. But not before. Understand?

They're close enough to see us now. I can see them. They're on the water, they're coming closer. They're going to see us soon. It's going to happen and we're going to be ready for it when it does.

Donatello — you stay here, you stay exactly where you are. No matter what. Not until I say.

DaVinci — come here. Just walk over. Don't say anything yet. Just stand here with me. We're not doing the group huddle. We're standing. Side by side. Just us. And you're not saying anything, or smiling, or looking excited. We're two people between the boat and the survivors, and we're not going to be the ones who give them a clue about what's going on out here until they're here and we're ready.

Michelangelo — you're not going to be the first one in the water. I don't care how long you've been staring at it, you're not. You stay here until I say so. Understand? No matter what.

Donatello — I'm going to be moving in five minutes. When I do you move with me. You stay close to me, you keep looking at me and not anything else, and you keep it simple. I know the plan. You know the plan. We're two people between them and the rest of this group, and we're going to hold it together until they're here.

DaVinci — you stay here, stand with me like you're not saying anything, you're not smiling, and you're not excited. I'm going to be moving in five minutes and then you move with me. Understand? Not before.

Michelangelo — you're not going to be the first one in the water. No matter what. Stay here until I say so.

*pauses, looks at the horizon, then over at Donatello. *

DaVinci — are we good?

records.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
records.response_truth:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on then — stay close, same as you have done since the start.

You know, when we landed I thought you were the one I'd have to carry through this. Turns out you were paying attention to everything the whole time, flagging things no one else was catching, asking the questions the rest of us were too busy to stop and ask. That's not nothing. That's actually quite a lot.

So yeah. We go together. Same as everything else out here.

After you.
records.response_pred:
Yeah. I'll follow you.

You know — you're not going to forget any of this, are you? I mean that honestly. Not the crash or the rain or the hunger, but the way the group held together when it mattered. That's not easy and it's not something you just do.

Write it up. Do the report. But also — keep the flowers in there.

I need to go home and think about it for a few days. I'll see you on the other side of that.
